title: What is not allowed
html:
Each entry names the error, the rule it breaks and where that rule lives, and a failing instance whose conclusion is marked true or false: a wrong argument can reach either.

  1. Verifying instances and concluding “for all”. Breaks ∀I, which needs one proof about a fresh name (@def-rules-universal, Section 4.4). Instance: n2−n+11 is prime for n=0,1,…,10 (the values are 11,11,13,17,23,31,41,53,67,83,101), “so it is prime for every n∈N”. False: at n=11 the value is 121=112.
  2. A witness that depends on a variable introduced later, while uniformity is claimed. Breaks the side conditions of ∃E and ∀I: a witness δ0 obtained inside the box of x0 may not leave it (Section 4.10, @exm-converse-fails). Instance: “x2 is continuous at every x, with δ=min{1,ε/(2|x|+1)}; so one δ for each ε serves every x, and x2 is uniformly continuous on R”. False (@exm-square-not-uniform).
  3. Treating the name from ∃E as arbitrary. Breaks the side condition of ∀I: the witness appears in the open assumption of its box (@def-rules-existential, Section 4.6). Instance: “Some element of A is positive; let x be such an element. Since x was arbitrary, every element of A is positive.” False for A={−1,1}.
  4. Reusing one witness name for two ∃E’s. Breaks the fresh-name condition: the second name may not appear in an open assumption, and the first box’s assumption mentions it (Section 4.6, @exm-sum-of-evens). Sibling boxes may share a name. Instance: “m and n are even, so m=2k and n=2k for an integer k; hence m=n”. False: m=2, n=4.
  5. Proving the converse. Breaks →I, whose box opens with the hypothesis, not the conclusion (@def-rules-implication, Section 1.5). Instance: “If x2>1, then x>1: suppose x>1; then x2>x>1.” False: x=−2. Argument B of Section 1.1 makes the same move with a true conclusion.
  6. Affirming the consequent; denying the antecedent. Not rules: P→Q with Q gives no P, and with ¬P gives no ¬Q. Each pattern has a refuting row, so no derivation exists (@cor-refuting-row, Section 3.5): @exm-affirming-the-consequent, and for denying the row P false, Q true. Instances: “a multiple of 4 is even and 6 is even, so 6 is a multiple of 4”; “… and 6 is not a multiple of 4, so 6 is not even”. Both false.
  7. A missing case. Breaks ∨E, which needs one box for each disjunct (@def-rules-disjunction, Section 1.7). Instance: “|x|>0 for every real x: every real x has x>0, x=0 or x<0; if x>0, |x|=x>0; if x<0, |x|=−x>0”. False: the case x=0 was dropped, and |0|=0.
  8. Cases that do not exhaust. Breaks ∨E, whose first input must be a disjunction already derived (Section 1.7). Instance: “x2≥x for every real x: either x≥1 or x≤0; in the first case x2=x⋅x≥x, in the second x2≥0≥x”. False: x=1/2 satisfies neither case, and 1/4<1/2.
  9. Citing a line that is not available: the goal itself (circular reasoning), a result proved later, or a general “fact” neither proved nor a declared premise. Breaks @def-derivation: every line is a premise, an assumption, or a rule applied to available lines (Section 1.5). Instances: “if n2 is even, then n is even: suppose n2 is even; since n is even, …” (true, and circular); “x<1, so x2<1, since squaring preserves <” (false: x=−2).
  10. Using an assumption after its box has closed. Breaks the scope rule of @def-derivation (Section 1.5). Instance: “Suppose n is even, say n=2k; then n2=4k2. Hence if n is even, 4∣n2. Now n2=4k2, so 4∣n2 for every integer n.” False: n=1. Proof D below makes the same move with a true conclusion.
  11. A wrong negation. An RAA box opened with a statement that is not the negation of the goal; a bound negated instead of a quantifier (@prp-bounded-quantifier-negation); the negation of φ→ψ written as an implication, ¬φ→¬ψ or φ→¬ψ, instead of φ∧¬ψ (@prp-negated-implication). Breaks RAA, which closes only a box opened with ¬φ (Section 2.5), or the laws of Section 4.9. Instances: “if x>2, then x2>4” is “refuted” because “if x≤2, then x2≤4” holds at x=0 (false: both are true at x=0, so one is not the negation of the other); “an=0 does not converge to 0, since some ε≤0 has |an−0|≥ε for all n” (false).
